accuracy.evidence: Fungi are presented as their own kingdom, not plants: no chlorophyll, no photosynthesis, feeding by releasing enzymes and absorbing nutrients from dead material. Mould grows from airborne spores, mushrooms are fruiting bodies of an underground network, yeast is a fungus, and the advice not to eat mouldy bread or wild mushrooms matches food safety guidance (USDA, NHS) and the death cap warning.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the four ideas young children most often hold: mould is dirt or the food changing colour rather than a living thing, a mushroom is a plant because it grows from the ground, mould appears from nowhere instead of from spores, and a wild mushroom that looks like a shop one is safe to eat. Each is answered in the lab, the text and a challenge tag.

lab_distinct.evidence: The flagmould lab has five different young-child activities: a day slider that grows mould spots on bread from day 0 to day 7, a two-box fungus or plant sort, a tap hunt for the four places fungi grow, dragging a mushroom onto a leaf, log and apple core that crumble into soil, and a safe or not safe sort. It passed the shingle check against every flag lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Each idea is seen before it is named. The child watches the spots spread day by day before being told mould is alive, sees the leaf, log and core shrink into a soil pile after the fungus lands, and only then reads the rule that fungi break dead things down. Every step ends with one short, concrete sentence a five year old can repeat.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions are locked before each task, each with a tempting wrong option: what the bread will look like after a week (same as now is the trap), whether a mushroom is a plant (yes is the trap for a ground-grower), and what happens to a dead leaf when a fungus grows on it. The child's own guess is shown again next to what happened.

challenge_feedback.evidence: The challenge rotates simple picture questions and every wrong option has a tag with its own reply: dirt and colour for not seeing mould as alive, plant and animal for grouping errors, eat for unsafe choices, clean for thinking mould grows on bare plates, nothing and magic for the spores idea, and baker for thinking mould is added to bread.

readability.evidence: The kid text uses very short sentences and everyday words and scores well under the family kid limit on Flesch-Kincaid, while the adult text scores about grade 9.6, inside the 10.5 allowance. Big tap targets, one instruction per lab step and words such as fungus, mould, spores and decomposer are each introduced with a picture.

no_filler.evidence: Each paragraph carries a fact, a safety rule or a named mistake. The adult text states plainly that fungi are not a named statutory objective at ages 5 to 7, ties the topic to Year 1 and 2 living, dead and never alive and micro-habitats, and points forward to NGSS 5-LS2-1 decomposers and Year 6 classification, without restating ideas.

mobile.evidence: Walked on iPhone 13 and desktop in the browser gate. The day slider, the drag of the mushroom and the tap hunt all use A.gest so touch and mouse both work, each drag also has a Next or tap button alternative, and the young class keeps targets large and the text big enough on a small phone.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core reported no violations in light or dark theme. The canvas has an aria-label, each object is labelled with a word as well as a drawing, nothing relies on colour alone because mould spots and soil are also counted and named, and all colours come from A.col so contrast holds in both themes.

sources: DfE (2013) National curriculum in England: science programmes of study, Year 2 living things and their habitats (living, dead and never alive; micro-habitats) and Year 6 classifying living things into broad groups including micro-organisms
NGSS 5-LS2-1: develop a model to describe the movement of matter among plants, animals, decomposers and the environment
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew, State of the World's Plants and Fungi (2018): fungi as a separate kingdom and their role as decomposers
USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service, Molds on Food: discard soft foods such as bread with visible mould; NHS guidance on wild mushroom poisoning
